design_decisions.change: Every Ready-blocker and gate is tagged to one of two tracks. The three-liner/letter-class track reuses high-b-to-low-c's structure closely (bands, category floors, unconditional hours gates) with only a one-point rise in thresholds.ready.total_min. The two-liner track adds six NEW conditional gates (see 'v1-two-liner-branch-is-gate-conditional-not-question-conditional') that only evaluate when is_2_liner:yes, built on the Lindenstruth survey and the Lobb/Janaway skill list.
design_decisions.reason: knowledge/steps/low-c-to-high-c.md opens by naming these as two things sources conflate, and knowledge/disagreements.md point 4 instructs treating 2-liner-ness as its own independent hard-gate trigger, separate from the EN letter. Averaging the two tracks into one threshold would understate the letter-class fuzziness and understate the 2-liner evidence in opposite directions at once.

source.cites: "Treat 'is this a 2-liner' as its own independent hard-gate trigger, separate from the EN letter. A pilot asking about an EN-C-certified 2-liner should still be asked the stricter 2-liner-specific questions... not just the standard low-C/high-C questions."
source.note: config/questions/low-c-to-high-c.json's design_notes record the same decision from the question-authoring side.

design_decisions.change: app/upgrade/lib/scoreEngine.ts has no support for conditionally skipping questions — every question in a step is shown to every pilot. So is_2_liner is asked first, the five two-liner-specific skill questions (pitch_control, cravat_recovery, frontal_collapse_energy, ears_deflation, plus speed_bar's existing scale) are asked of everyone, and only the GATES built on them are conditional, using the existing all_of/any_of + question/answer_in system — e.g. a gate's when can be {"all_of": [{"question": "is_2_liner", "answer_in": ["yes"]}, {"question": "cravat_recovery", "answer_in": ["never", "theory_only"]}]}. A three-liner pilot still answers these questions and their answers still carry scored weight (cravats and frontals are not two-liner-only events), but none of the six two-liner-conditional gates can fire for them.
design_decisions.reason: Deliberate engine-compatibility choice, not an oversight. True conditional question-skipping would need app/engine changes outside this rubric's scope.
design_decisions.owner_note: This step is the first one that would genuinely benefit from real conditional skipping — a three-liner pilot currently answers 5 questions (cravat_recovery, frontal_collapse_energy, ears_deflation, pitch_control, collapse_training_access) whose gates can never apply to them, which adds length without adding safety value for that branch. Worth considering for a future engine change if more 2-liner-gated steps get built (this ladder only has one more 2-liner-relevant step, high-C to D, so the case is moderate, not urgent).

This is a single-source figure (knowledge/disagreements.md point 2), but it comes from a survey-backed expert with a documented bad outcome attached, which is a different quality of evidence from most single-source hours figures in this knowledge base.

design_decisions.change: Six gates fire only when is_2_liner:yes: two_liner_thin_previous_category (current_wing_time:under_20), two_liner_cravat_untested (cravat_recovery: never/theory_only), two_liner_pitch_control_weak (pitch_control: not_thought_about/react_unreliably), two_liner_frontal_energy_untested (frontal_collapse_energy: never_thought/theory_only), two_liner_ears_unsure (ears_deflation:unsure), two_liner_passive_bar_use (speed_bar:stomp_it_on).
design_decisions.reason: Each traces to a specific, named 2-liner finding. cravat_recovery and pitch_control: the two skills both Lobb and Janaway agree matter (point 1). frontal_collapse_energy: Lobb's third must-have SIV skill (managing frontal-collapse energy). ears_deflation: Lindenstruth's survey found ~25% of pilots moving to a two-liner C struggled with ear deflation on the shorter line set specifically, and names it as a warning sign. two_liner_passive_bar_use: Lindenstruth names relying on the bar passively, without active brake management, as a false-security pattern specifically flagged in his red-flag list.

source.cites: "A specific, named red-flag list for 2-liners... inability to confidently deploy 'ears' (wingtip deflation) on the specific new wing; relying on the speed bar passively without active brake management during acceleration (which he says creates false security rather than real control); skipping familiarisation flights in benign conditions before flying the new wing in thermic or high terrain."
source.note: Skipping familiarisation (richiesadventures, Lindenstruth) is handled as a suggestion (learning_curve_willingness already carries weight) rather than a seventh gate, since no source frames it as a single-answer red flag the way the other six are.

Whether the six two-liner-conditional gates are individually right. They are new territory for this knowledge base and each rests on a single survey or a pair of expert voices (Lindenstruth, Lobb, Janaway) rather than the multi-source convergence some earlier gates have. The evidence quality is good (a 287-pilot survey is unusually strong for this knowledge base) but it is still one survey.

Whether true conditional question-skipping is worth an engine change, given a three-liner pilot currently answers 5 two-liner-oriented questions whose gates can never apply to them. See 'v1-two-liner-branch-is-gate-conditional-not-question-conditional'.

meta.method: Each answer has a score from 0 to 1. Within a category, score = sum(weight x answer_score) / sum(weight of answered, scored questions) x 100. Total = 0.53 x skills + 0.47 x psychological, then bonuses are added and the total is clamped to 0-100. Gates are applied last and override the total.

gates.message: This is the one skill two experts who disagree about almost everything else agree matters before a two-liner. Fewer lines give collapsing fabric more room to tangle, so cravats are more likely here than on the wing you're on, and clearing one isn't the same instinct as clearing an ordinary collapse. Practised, deliberately, over water or with a coach, is what this needs.

source.cites: Lobb and Janaway both name cravat clearing as a real priority.
source.note: Two-liner-conditional.

gates.message: This is the other skill both experts agree on, whatever they disagree about elsewhere. A two-liner hands you pitch movement sooner and wants a lighter touch than the wing you're on — catching a surge on the brakes, holding it on the rear risers while you're on bar, easing off before it dives. Worth building deliberately rather than meeting for the first time on the new wing.

source.cites: Pitch control named by both Lobb and Janaway.
source.note: Two-liner-conditional.

gates.message: Managing the energy that comes out of a frontal collapse is on the short list of things one detailed analysis expects before a two-liner. It's the same skill as pitch control at its loudest — worth meeting deliberately, with height or over water, rather than for the first time on the new wing.

source.cites: Malin Lobb names frontal-collapse energy management as a must-have SIV skill.
source.note: Two-liner-conditional.

gates.message: In a survey of nearly 300 pilots flying two-line C wings, about a quarter had real difficulty getting ears in on the shorter line set — and the survey names it as one of its specific warning signs. Worth being confident with ears on the wing you're on before relying on them on a new one with a different pull.

source.cites: Lindenstruth's survey, the ~25% figure.
source.note: Two-liner-conditional.

gates.message: The same survey names leaning on the bar passively, without working the brakes as the wing accelerates, as a specific warning sign — it gives a feeling of security rather than actual control, on exactly the wings where that control matters most. Easing the bar on while watching the pitch, and trimming the pressure as you go, is the habit worth building first.

source.cites: Lindenstruth's red-flag list.
source.note: Two-liner-conditional.

gates.message: By your own account, your current wing hasn't yet been the thing stopping you — and that's the clearest marker this step's research gives. A later wing is very unlikely to change that on its own. Usually it means there's performance still sitting in the wing you've got, waiting to be collected, which is the cheapest kind there is.

gates.message: A high-C or a two-liner won't make rough air easier — at this step the trade runs the other way more clearly than anywhere below. What does make rough air easier is thermal hours, active flying, and knowing exactly what you'd do if the wing folded. All of that is available on the wing you already have.

critical_check_floor:current_wing_time.message: One thing is holding this back: time on the wing you're on now. This is the single best-evidenced figure in the whole research for this step — a pilot who surveyed nearly 300 two-liner owners treats under about 20 hours on your previous category as a genuine warning sign, with a real case behind it. You're not quite there yet. More time on the wing you already trust, flown properly rather than just logged, is what moves this.

source.cites: Lindenstruth's survey.
source.note: Reached by the 20_50 band on the three-liner track; under_20 is a hard gate on the two-liner track.

critical_check_floor:collapse_practice.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the one place this step genuinely asks more of you than the wing you're on does. The certification wording for this class assumes precise, deliberate input to recover from a collapse. Wingovers, a controlled spiral, a bigger asymmetric with someone watching — the suggestion below has the order to do it in.

source.cites: Carried forward from high-b-to-low-c.

critical_check_floor:pitch_control.message: One thing is holding this back: damping a surge or a dive when the wing moves on you. Two voices who disagree about a lot of this agree that pitch control is one of the skills worth having before a two-liner specifically — and it matters on a demanding three-liner too. Catching it on the brakes, then holding it on the rear risers while you're on bar, is the progression worth practising.

source.cites: Lobb and Janaway both name pitch control.

critical_check_floor:cravat_recovery.message: One thing is holding this back: clearing a cravat. It's the other skill both of those voices agree on. Never having had one isn't the problem by itself — not having practised clearing one deliberately is. A session over water with a coach is the direct fix.

source.cites: Lobb and Janaway both name cravat clearing.

critical_check_floor:wing_limiting_evide.message: One thing is holding this back: by your own account, your current wing hasn't clearly been the thing stopping you yet. That usually means there's performance still sitting in it, which is worth collecting first.

source.cites: Carried forward from high-b-to-low-c.

critical_check_floor:active_piloting.message: One thing is holding this back: what your hands do when the air gets bumpy. This class rewards precise, continuous input more than the wing you're on does. Light, friendly bumps are the place to build the habit, not the big days.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:thermal_turn_contro.message: One thing is holding this back: thermalling that works but isn't yet fully under your control. The suggestion below has specific things to drill.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:response_when_rough.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't nerves — that part is normal. It's what happens next: tightening up and waiting it out rather than carrying on flying the wing. That builds like any other habit.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:flying_frequency.message: One thing is holding this back: how often you're actually getting in the air right now. Two or three times a month, in whatever conditions you can get, changes this and several other answers with it.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:collapse_experience.message: One thing is holding this back, and it isn't that you froze — that's the normal starting point, not a character flaw. It's that the reaction hasn't been tested yet. It's trainable, and the wing you're on is a better one to learn on than the one you're shopping for.

source.cites: Carried forward.

critical_check_floor:reserve_familiarity.message: One thing is holding this back, and it's the quickest to fix: not being certain you could find the reserve handle in a hurry. Two minutes in a hang check changes this permanently.

source.cites: Carried forward.

unevidenced_core_checks:thermal_turn_con.message: One thing is unevidenced rather than weak. You've said thermalling mostly hasn't come up, so it scores as neutral, not against you. But there isn't a reading of the guidance for this step — on either track — that a soaring-only pilot clears, so this result doesn't move just because your plans stay local. Worth knowing plainly rather than finding out later.

always_output.instructor_recommendation: Whatever this says, run it past an instructor or coach who has seen you fly — and test-fly the specific wing before you buy it. That matters more here than almost anywhere else on the ladder: two wings with the same letter can ask very different things of you depending on whether they're a two-liner, and someone who knows both you and the specific wing is doing work no form can do.
always_output.disclaimer: This is a self-assessment tool based on published guidance from national associations, manufacturers, retailers and instructors. It isn't an instructor, it can't see you fly, and it isn't a safety clearance. Wing choice is your responsibility and your instructor's advice always comes first.
always_output.methodology_note: This step is really two assessments wearing one label. The letter-class boundary — a conventional low-C to a conventional high-C — is thin and genuinely bidirectional: almost nobody writes about it, and one manufacturer markets the same kind of wing both as a step up and a step down. Moving onto a two-liner is different. That's the best-corroborated material anywhere in this research, including a structured survey of nearly 300 two-liner pilots, and it points at specific, named things worth having in place first — not back-flying, where two respected voices disagree, but cravat clearing and pitch control, where they agree. So this assessment asks which of the two you're actually looking at, and reads the rest of your answers more strictly if the answer is a two-liner. Every weight and gate links back to the criterion it came from.
